patterns.title: Inflated forecasts, consultants and insiders
patterns.summary:
John Perkins's 2004 book Confessions of an Economic Hit Man says that Chas. T. Main, a Boston engineering firm, paid him in the 1970s to produce high growth and electricity-demand forecasts, so that countries such as Indonesia would borrow large sums and spend them on contracts with US firms (he names Bechtel, Halliburton, Stone & Webster and Brown & Root). Records confirm the outline of his career: he joined Main in early 1971 as a junior economist after the Peace Corps in Ecuador, and Parsons Corporation bought Main in 1985 (Boston Magazine, 2006). Records do not confirm his central claims: that the National Security Agency screened him, that a Main consultant trained him as an "economic hit man", or that US agents killed Panama's Omar Torrijos and Ecuador's Jaime Roldós. Official inquiries in both countries blamed pilot error, though later inquiries left questions open. The US State Department called much of the book a fabrication in February 2006, and his former boss Einar Greve denied the NSA link.

The underlying problem Perkins describes, forecasts and lending pressure that ran ahead of reality, is documented by insiders and by the lenders' own reviews. IMF economist Davison Budhoo resigned in 1988 saying the Fund had inflated Trinidad and Tobago's rise in unit labour costs (164.7% for 1980-85 against his 66.1%); a Trinidad government committee (the Bourne Committee) found the IMF figure even more inflated, while the IMF denied any error in March 1989. The World Bank's 1992 Wapenhans report found the share of Bank projects with major problems rose from 11% (1981) to 20% (1991) and blamed an "approval culture". In Pakistan, a 1994 policy assumed about 7% yearly demand growth and drew some 4,500 MW of private plants, many backed by the World Bank Group; demand grew more slowly and left surplus capacity. Indonesia's Paiton plant was signed at just over 8 US cents/kWh and renegotiated after 1997. IMF studies found growth forecasts in IMF-supported programs leaned optimistic (Baqir, Ramcharan and Sahay 2005), though a 2014 review found the bias weak except in very large programs. Former World Bank chief economist Joseph Stiglitz wrote in April 2000 that IMF and US Treasury programs worsened the 1997-98 Asian crisis.

countries.note: Seat of the IMF and World Bank (Washington) and home of Chas. T. Main (Boston), bought by Parsons of Pasadena in 1985 (Boston Magazine, 2006). The US Treasury ran the Saudi-funded JECOR program, which by 1978 had contracts with over 100 US firms worth about US$140 million (GAO, 1979).

Perkins says Main pushed for a Java electricity forecast of about 17% yearly growth and that forecaster Howard Parker, who called 6% reasonable, was fired (Confessions, ch. 5); no Main records confirm this. Separately documented: the Paiton private power contract paid just over 8 US cents/kWh, the state utility PLN sought renegotiation in 1999, and a price under 5 cents was agreed for part of the output in 2002 (Wikipedia, citing Jakarta Post); an MIT thesis (Yuliyanti, 2001) points to a high take-or-pay share and an over-optimistic demand projection. MIGA, a World Bank affiliate, gave guarantees. Stiglitz (2000) says food and fuel subsidies were cut under the 1997-98 IMF program.

The 1994 power policy issued letters of support for 34 projects over 9,000 MW; about 20 plants with roughly 4,500 MW reached financial close, on an assumed demand growth near 7% a year. Demand grew more slowly and left excess capacity; the Bank Group had advised capping it near 2,000 MW and was involved in 11 of 16 plants (88% of private MW). Government corruption allegations in 1998 against Hubco (1,292 MW, US$1.6 billion) ended in a December 2000 tariff settlement (Fraser, World Bank, 2005).

IMF staff economist Davison Budhoo, on the 1985-87 missions, said the 1986 mission overstated the 1980-85 rise in real unit labour costs (164.7% against 66.1%). The government's Bourne Committee upheld him; the Levitt investigation upheld the substance but questioned its weight. The IMF denied error in a 20 March 1989 telex. Loans followed in 1989 and 1990 after more austerity (Multinational Monitor, 1990).

Perkins says Omar Torrijos was killed by a bomb placed by US interests (Confessions, pp. 156-157). Torrijos died on 31 July 1981 when a Panamanian Air Force Twin Otter hit Marta Hill near Coclesito; a 1983 inquiry blamed the pilots and found no explosive residue. Relatives rejected it, the case was later declared unsolved, and the files were lost in the 1989 US invasion (Wikipedia, 1981 Twin Otter crash).

Perkins served in the Peace Corps here 1968-70 and says Jaime Roldós was assassinated for opposing foreign oil interests (Confessions, ch. 26). Roldós died on 24 May 1981 in an Air Force Beechcraft King Air crash in Loja; the 1981 Air Force inquiry found navigational pilot error and ruled out a mid-air explosion. Inquiries in 1981 and 1990-92 found contradictions but no conclusion, and the case was reopened in 2013 (Wikipedia; El Comercio).

Perkins describes a plan to recycle Saudi oil money into US-built modernization (Confessions, ch. 15). The structure is documented: the US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation (JECOR) was set up on 8 June 1974; by September 1978 Saudi Arabia had deposited US$250 million in a Treasury trust account (GAO, 1979). Saudi funding meant no US appropriation was needed (Middle East Institute, 2009). Perkins's own role is not confirmed.
Perkins writes about Iran in chapter 18 and ties his job to the 1953 coup. Boston Magazine (2006) reports that Main had contracts in Iran but gives no detail; no project record was found.

Stiglitz (New Republic, 17 April 2000) says Thailand followed IMF advice most closely in 1997-98 and did worse than Malaysia and South Korea; he argues austerity and high interest rates were the wrong cure for a private-debt crisis. This is his account as an insider.

Stiglitz (2000) says early-1990s financial opening in East Asia, partly pushed by the US Treasury, drew short-term money that fed the crisis, and that Korea recovered by taking a more independent path.

Stiglitz (2000) says rapid privatization and capital opening let oligarchs strip state assets. The World Bank's own evaluation (OED, Berney 2002) states early expectations of rapid reform were highly unrealistic; two oil rehabilitation loans of US$1.1 billion disbursed US$760.5 million and were rated unsatisfactory.

timeline.event: John Perkins, 26, joins Chas. T. Main in Boston as a junior economist.
The US and Saudi Arabia set up JECOR on 8 June, a Treasury-run program paid for by Saudi deposits.
JECOR's Saudi trust account reaches US$250 million; contracts with over 100 US firms total about US$140 million.
Ecuador's President Jaime Roldós dies in a plane crash on 24 May; the Air Force inquiry finds navigational pilot error.
Panama's leader Omar Torrijos dies in a Twin Otter crash near Coclesito on 31 July.
A Panamanian inquiry blames the Torrijos crash on the pilots and finds no explosive residue.
Parsons Corporation of Pasadena buys Chas. T. Main.
An IMF mission reports a 164.7% rise in Trinidad and Tobago's unit labour costs for 1980-85; Budhoo later puts it at 66.1%.
IMF economist Davison Budhoo resigns with a public letter of over 100 pages alleging deliberate statistical errors.
The IMF denies in a 20 March telex that any error or manipulation of Trinidad data occurred.
A World Bank review of about 300 power projects financed 1965-83 finds declining power-sector performance.
The Wapenhans report finds projects with major problems rose from 11% to 20% over 1981-91 and cites an approval culture.
Ecuador's Granda inquiry into the Roldós crash issues a 26-volume report with inconsistencies but no conclusion.
Pakistan's March 1994 power policy issues letters of support for 34 private projects over 9,000 MW.
The US GAO reports the Bank's own task force blamed a culture focused on loan approval and disbursement.
Pakistan issues termination notices to private power plants holding about two-thirds of contracted capacity, citing corruption.
Former World Bank chief economist Joseph Stiglitz publishes his critique of the IMF's Asia programs in the New Republic.
Indonesia and Paiton's owners agree a price just under 5 US cents/kWh for part of the output, down from just over 8.
An IMF Staff Papers study of 94 programs (1989-2002) finds an optimistic bias in growth forecasts.
Boston Magazine finds Perkins's career outline real but his documentation thin, and former colleagues dispute key scenes.
An IMF evaluation background paper of 103 programs (2002-11) finds only weak growth optimism, significant in exceptional-access programs.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says the National Security Agency tested and screened him before Chas. T. Main hired him (ch. 1).
claims_per_author.status: Unconfirmed. The State Department (February 2006) said there is no documentary or testimonial evidence and that the NSA has no economic mission; Einar Greve said he knew no one from the NSA (Wikipedia; Boston Magazine 2006).

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says Main vice president Einar Greve recruited him (ch. 1).
claims_per_author.status: Partly confirmed: Greve confirms he recruited Perkins to Main and once told the Tucson Citizen the story was basically true, but later disputed where they met, the NSA link and the Ecuador letters (Boston Magazine 2006).

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says a Main consultant, Claudine Martin, trained him as an "economic hit man" whose job was to win big loans that would return to US firms (ch. 2).
claims_per_author.status: Unconfirmed. Greve called the library episode fiction; Boston Magazine (2006) notes doubts that she existed and says Perkins offered a thin package of evidence.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says loans built this way were spent on contracts with Bechtel, Halliburton, Stone & Webster and Brown & Root (ch. 2).
claims_per_author.status: No project-by-project record linking these firms to Main forecasts was found. Boston Magazine reports a separate allegation of a US$200 million Bechtel payment to a Saudi prince over the Riyadh airport contract, also unconfirmed.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says Main expected Java electricity forecasts of at least 17% yearly growth, and that forecaster Howard Parker, who said 7-9% was the historic ceiling, refused and was fired (ch. 5).
claims_per_author.status: Unconfirmed. Boston Magazine repeats it from Perkins; no Main forecast documents were found, and Parsons said it did not know where Main's records are.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says he helped design a plan to recycle Saudi oil money into US-built modernization (ch. 15).
claims_per_author.status: The structure is real: JECOR, created 1974, held US$250 million of Saudi deposits by 1978 and placed about US$140 million in contracts with US firms (GAO 1979). Perkins's personal role is not confirmed (Boston Magazine 2006).

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says Omar Torrijos was killed by a bomb planted by US interests (pp. 156-157; ch. 27).
claims_per_author.status: Contradicted by the 1983 Panamanian inquiry (pilot error, no explosive residue). Relatives alleged a cover-up; the case was later declared unsolved and files were lost in 1989 (Wikipedia, Twin Otter crash).

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says Jaime Roldós was assassinated for opposing foreign oil companies and creditors (Preface; ch. 26).
claims_per_author.status: Contradicted by the 1981 Ecuadorian Air Force inquiry (navigational pilot error, mid-air explosion ruled out). Later inquiries (1981, 1990-92) found contradictions but no conclusion; the case was reopened in 2013 (Wikipedia; El Comercio).

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says that where economic hit men failed, as in Iraq and Venezuela, CIA-linked "jackals" stepped in (Prologue; ch. 31, 33).
claims_per_author.status: No record found to confirm or test this.

claims_per_author.author: John Perkins
claims_per_author.work: Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004)
claims_per_author.claim: Perkins says he rose to chief economist at Main and left out of conscience.
claims_per_author.status: The New York Times found the arc of his career described accurately (as quoted by Wikipedia). His former supervisor Frank Fullerton said he left because he thought he was worth more (Boston Magazine 2006).

claims_per_author.author: Joseph Stiglitz
claims_per_author.work: New Republic essay on the world economic crisis (17 April 2000)
claims_per_author.claim: Stiglitz says the IMF, with the US Treasury, applied austerity and high interest rates to East Asia in 1997-98 when the problem was private debt, and that this deepened the downturn.
claims_per_author.status: One insider's account. Stiglitz was World Bank chief economist until late 1999. The IMF's view is not in the opened text; a 2014 IMF evaluation paper on forecasts did not test this claim.

claims_per_author.author: Davison Budhoo
claims_per_author.work: Enough Is Enough, open letter to Michel Camdessus (1988)
claims_per_author.claim: Budhoo says the IMF used deliberate statistical fraud to impose policies on Trinidad and Tobago and other countries.
claims_per_author.status: For Trinidad's unit labour cost figure, the government's Bourne Committee upheld him and the Levitt investigation upheld the substance; the IMF denied any error (Multinational Monitor 1990). His wider claim of systematic fraud elsewhere is not confirmed.

uncertain: No record found shows what Chas. T. Main actually forecast or built in Indonesia, Panama, Ecuador, Colombia or Saudi Arabia; the firm's surviving archive at Northeastern covers 1975-77 and lists only Turkey and Jordan Valley work.

Whether US agencies had any role in the 1981 deaths of Torrijos and Roldós is unproven; official inquiries blamed pilot error, and later Ecuadorian inquiries could not reach a conclusion partly because the plane carried no black box.

Critics dispute Perkins's whole thesis: Sebastian Mallaby (Washington Post, 2006) called his basic contentions wrong, and Niall Ferguson (2008) noted US lending to Ecuador and Panama was too small a share to kill for (both as reported by Wikipedia).
The State Department rebuttal "Confessions - or Fantasies - of an Economic Hit Man?" is dated February 2006, not 2005; its text is known here only through Wikipedia's summary.

IMF growth-forecast optimism is contested: Baqir, Ramcharan and Sahay (2005, 94 programs 1989-2002) found a bias that survived controls, while Luna (2014, 103 programs 2002-11) found it weak and not significant except in exceptional-access programs.

Whether Pakistan's 1994 private-power surplus came from inflated forecasts or from slower growth is not settled; the World Bank paper says demand grew more slowly than the roughly 7% assumed but does not measure the forecast error.
The IMF never publicly reviewed Budhoo's charges; it denied error in 1989 and dropped the disputed index for a different measure.

dropped.idea: Main's documented projects in Indonesia, Panama, Ecuador, Colombia and Saudi Arabia
dropped.why: No archive or World Bank record naming Main in these countries was found; two World Bank archive files checked did not mention Main.
Only the chapter title (ch. 21) was read; no record of a Main project in Colombia was found.

dropped.idea: Stone & Webster, Halliburton and Bechtel project links
dropped.why: No primary record tying these firms to forecast-driven loans was found; only a reported, unconfirmed Bechtel bribe allegation.

dropped.idea: World Bank Operations Evaluation findings on over-optimistic demand forecasts
dropped.why: No OED report stating this was opened; the 1989 power lending review abstract shows declining performance but does not mention forecasts.

dropped.idea: New York Times and Washington Post reviews of Perkins in full
dropped.why: Pages could not be opened; their findings are reported only through Wikipedia.

dropped.idea: Stiglitz phrase on third-rank students from first-rate universities
dropped.why: Not found in the article text that was opened.

patterns.title: The economists' pipeline
patterns.summary:
US universities, foundations and aid agencies trained economists from borrowing countries who later ran finance ministries, central banks and planning agencies while those countries took IMF and World Bank programs. In March 1956 Chile's Catholic University signed a cooperation agreement with the University of Chicago, funded by the US government through the International Cooperation Administration; about 100 Chileans trained between 1957 and 1970. After the 1973 coup they held the economy, finance, planning and labour ministries (Sergio de Castro, finance 1977-82; Hernán Büchi, finance 1985-89). In Indonesia the Ford Foundation sent University of Indonesia students to UC Berkeley from 1957; after 1966 this group ran planning (Widjojo Nitisastro, Bappenas 1967-83) and finance (Ali Wardhana, 1968-83) and led delegations to the IMF, World Bank and the aid group IGGI.

From the 1980s, US-based advisers worked inside governments. Harvard's Jeffrey Sachs advised Bolivia in 1985 (Decree 21060, backed by US$57 million of IMF credit), Poland in 1989-90 and Russia's Yeltsin government from late 1991 to January 1994. USAID gave Harvard's Institute for International Development (HIID) about US$40 million for Russia from 1992 without competition (GAO 1996); the US government sued, and in 2005 Harvard agreed to pay US$26.5 million, Andrei Shleifer US$2 million and Jonathan Hay up to US$2 million, without admitting liability, after a 2004 ruling that Shleifer and Hay broke conflict-of-interest rules. In 1989 John Williamson listed ten reforms that the IMF, World Bank and US Treasury backed, which he called the Washington Consensus. Mexico's cabinet under Carlos Salinas (Harvard) included Pedro Aspe (MIT), Ernesto Zedillo (Yale) and Jaime Serra Puche (Yale, Stanford); Argentina's Domingo Cavallo (Harvard PhD 1977) ran the 1991 convertibility plan.

countries.note: University of Chicago (Chile program from 1956), UC Berkeley with Ford Foundation funds (Indonesia, from 1957), Harvard (Sachs; HIID's US$40 million USAID Russia award), MIT and Yale (Mexican ministers), and Williamson's 1989 Washington Consensus list at PIIE.

About 100 Catholic University economists trained 1957-70 under the 1956 Chicago agreement (Wikipedia; Stabili 2021). Under Pinochet they held finance (de Castro 1977-82; Büchi 1985-89), economy (Baraona 1976-79), labour and pensions (Piñera 1978-80) and planning and the central bank (Kast). Their program, El Ladrillo, was finished weeks before the 1973 coup.

Ford Foundation-backed Berkeley training began in 1957. After an August 1966 seminar, Suharto announced a stabilization program on 3 October 1966; inflation fell from about 650% (1966) to about 13% (1969). Widjojo headed Bappenas 1967-83 and led IGGI, Paris Club, IMF and World Bank delegations; Ali Wardhana (Berkeley PhD 1962) was finance minister 1968-83; Mohammad Sadli was first head of the investment board in 1967.

Reason (1989) lists President Salinas (Harvard), Treasury Secretary Pedro Aspe (MIT doctorate, a lead backer of privatization), Budget Secretary Ernesto Zedillo (Yale doctorate) and Commerce Secretary Jaime Serra Puche (Yale, Stanford). Sarah Babb's Managing Mexico (Princeton, 2001) traces how US-credentialed economists came to dominate policymaking.

Domingo Cavallo, Harvard PhD 1977, headed the central bank in 1982, was economy minister 1991-96 and introduced the 1991 dollar-backed convertibility plan; he returned in 2001 and resigned on 19 December 2001 after the deposit freeze (Group of Thirty; Biografías y Vidas). Wikipedia also lists Chicago-trained Adolfo Diz and Roque Fernández.

Decree 21060 of 29 August 1985 under President Paz Estenssoro, drawn up with adviser Jeffrey Sachs, devalued the peso by 93% and froze public wages; the IMF approved it with US$57 million in credit. Inflation, put at about 20,000% (Wikipedia) or 60,000% (IMF F&D), fell to 11% by 1987.

Poland's government approached Sachs in early 1989; he worked with Solidarity and Finance Minister Leszek Balcerowicz on the plan launched 1 January 1990 and argued for debt cancellation (IMF Finance & Development, 2012).

Sachs advised Yeltsin's government from late 1991 to January 1994. HIID received about US$40 million of USAID's US$325 million Russian privatization program (FY1992-96), helped create the Russian Privatization Center and drafted 3 of 9 core laws (GAO 1996). A US court found Shleifer and Hay liable under the False Claims Act in 2004; the 2005 settlement totalled at least US$31 million.
USAID gave HIID a US$1.5 million award in May 1996, scaled back from about US$6 million, on foreign policy grounds; GAO noted possible duplication with other donors (GAO 1996).

timeline.event: Chile's Catholic University and the University of Chicago sign a scientific cooperation agreement in March, with US government funds.
Ford Foundation-funded training of University of Indonesia economists at UC Berkeley begins.
Ali Wardhana completes his Berkeley PhD on monetary policy in Indonesia.
Suharto announces a stabilization program on 3 October based partly on the University of Indonesia economists' advice.
Widjojo Nitisastro becomes head of Indonesia's planning agency Bappenas, a post held until 1983.
Berkeley-trained Ali Wardhana becomes Indonesia's finance minister, serving until 1983.
Chicago-trained economists finish El Ladrillo, an economic program, weeks before the 11 September coup in Chile.
Milton Friedman visits Chile from 20 to 27 March; Pinochet then gives Chicago-trained economists key posts.
Sergio de Castro becomes Chile's finance minister, serving to 1982.
Bolivia issues Decree 21060 on 29 August, drawn up with Jeffrey Sachs; the IMF backs it with US$57 million.
John Williamson lists ten reforms backed by the IMF, World Bank and US Treasury and calls them the Washington Consensus.
Mexico's new cabinet includes US-trained Salinas, Aspe, Zedillo and Serra Puche.
Poland launches the Balcerowicz plan on 1 January, prepared with Sachs's advice.
Harvard-trained Domingo Cavallo becomes Argentina's economy minister and introduces the convertibility plan.
USAID makes a noncompetitive award to Harvard's HIID for Russia in December; it grows to US$40.4 million by 1995.
The US GAO reports minimal USAID oversight of HIID's legal reform work in Russia.
Cavallo resigns as Argentina's economy minister on 19 December after the deposit freeze.
Judge Douglas Woodlock finds Shleifer and Hay liable under the False Claims Act; Harvard is liable for breach of contract.
Harvard agrees to pay US$26.5 million, Shleifer US$2 million and Hay up to US$2 million, admitting no liability.

claims_per_author.author: Joseph Stiglitz
claims_per_author.work: New Republic essay on the world economic crisis (17 April 2000)
claims_per_author.claim: Stiglitz says Russia's rapid privatization and capital opening, advised from Washington, let oligarchs take state assets and drove poverty up sharply.
claims_per_author.status: One insider's view. The World Bank's OED (2002) separately says early expectations of rapid reform in Russia were highly unrealistic; HIID's advisers were not blamed for outcomes by GAO, which rated parts of their work successful.

claims_per_author.author: Milton and Rose Friedman
claims_per_author.work: Two Lucky People (memoir, 1998), as cited by Wikipedia
claims_per_author.claim: The Friedmans say Pinochet turned to the Chicago Boys in 1975 and put several in powerful posts.
claims_per_author.status: Consistent with the documented appointments (de Castro, finance, 1977-82; Baraona, economy, 1976-79).

claims_per_author.author: Andrei Shleifer and Harvard
claims_per_author.work: Statements on the 2005 settlement (Harvard Magazine; Harvard Crimson)
claims_per_author.claim: Harvard says it engaged in no institutional wrongdoing, and Shleifer says he would have won at trial.
claims_per_author.status: The court had already found Shleifer and Hay liable in 2004 and Harvard liable for breach of contract, while clearing Harvard of knowing fraud; the settlement contains no admission.

uncertain: The Church Committee staff report says the CIA funded a growing share, over 75% by 1972-73, of an opposition research organization in Chile; the opened text does not name it or link it to El Ladrillo, so CIA funding of the Chicago Boys' plan is not established here.
El Ladrillo's date is reported differently: Wikipedia's Chicago Boys page gives 1969 for an earlier program; the El ladrillo page and Edwards (via Econlib) place the final text in 1972-73.
Bolivia's peak inflation is given as about 20,000% (Wikipedia) and about 60,000% (IMF Finance & Development); the source of each figure differs.
Whether foreign training caused these policies or local politics did is argued, not settled; Babb (2001) stresses that national circumstances shape what economists do.
The link between Sachs's Harvard work and HIID's USAID Russia contract is not shown in the opened sources; GAO 1996 does not name Anatoly Chubais.
Mexican ministers' degrees come from one magazine article (Reason, 1989) plus Babb's general finding; individual degree records were not checked.
